Earth's rotation period relative to the [fixed stars](/wiki/Fixed_star "Fixed star"), called its *stellar day* by the [International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service](/wiki/International_Earth_Rotation_and_Reference_Systems_Service "International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service") (IERS), is 86,164.0989 seconds of mean solar time ([UT1](/wiki/UT1 "UT1")), or 23h 56m 4.0989s.[[2]](#cite_note-IERS-4)[[n 10]](#cite_note-Aoki-196) Earth's rotation period relative to the [precessing](/wiki/Precession_(astronomy) "Precession (astronomy)") or moving mean [March equinox](/wiki/March_equinox "March equinox") (when the Sun is at 90° on the equator), is 86,164.0905 seconds of mean solar time (UT1) (23h 56m 4.0905s).[[2]](#cite_note-IERS-4) Thus the sidereal day is shorter than the stellar day by about 8.4 ms.[[187]](#cite_note-seidelmann1992-197)

The regular dodecahedron is a polyhedron with twelve pentagonal faces, thirty edges, and twenty vertices.[[2]](#cite_note-sutton-2) It is one of the [Platonic solids](/wiki/Platonic_solid "Platonic solid"), a set of polyhedrons in which the faces are [regular polygons](/wiki/Regular_polygons "Regular polygons") that are [congruent](/wiki/Congruence_(geometry) "Congruence (geometry)") and the same number of faces meet at a vertex.[[3]](#cite_note-hs-3) This set of polyhedrons is named after [Plato](/wiki/Plato "Plato"). In *[Theaetetus](/wiki/Theaetetus_(dialogue) "Theaetetus (dialogue)")*, a dialogue of Plato, Plato hypothesized that the classical elements were made of the five uniform regular solids. Plato described the regular dodecahedron, obscurely remarked, "...the god used [it] for arranging the constellations on the whole heaven". The African bush elephant occurs in [sub-Saharan Africa](/wiki/Sub-Saharan_Africa "Sub-Saharan Africa") which includes [Uganda](/wiki/Uganda "Uganda"), [Kenya](/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), [Tanzania](/wiki/Tanzania "Tanzania"), [Botswana](/wiki/Botswana "Botswana"), [Zimbabwe](/wiki/Zimbabwe "Zimbabwe"), [Namibia](/wiki/Namibia "Namibia"), [Zambia](/wiki/Zambia "Zambia"), [Angola](/wiki/Angola "Angola"), [Malawi](/wiki/Malawi "Malawi"), [Mali](/wiki/Mali "Mali"), [Rwanda](/wiki/Rwanda "Rwanda"), [Mozambique](/wiki/Mozambique "Mozambique") and [South Africa](/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa"). It moves between a variety of habitats, including subtropical and [temperate forests](/wiki/Temperate_forest "Temperate forest"), dry and seasonally flooded [grasslands](/wiki/Grassland "Grassland"), woodlands, [wetlands](/wiki/Wetland "Wetland"), and agricultural land from sea level to mountain slopes. In Mali and Namibia, it also inhabits desert and semi-desert areas.[[2]](#cite_note-iucn-2)

Populations of African bush elephants are increasing in some areas such as the [Kruger National Park](/wiki/Kruger_National_Park "Kruger National Park"), where an annual growth of 4.2% was recorded between 2003 and 2015.[[27]](#cite_note-29) There are estimated to be at least 17,000 elephants in the park's vicinity, as of 2015–the most of any area in South Africa.[[28]](#cite_note-:3-30)[[29]](#cite_note-31) The increase in population occurred after the discontinuation of [culling](/wiki/Culling "Culling") in the mid-1990s.[[30]](#cite_note-32) This large elephant population is considered a problem to both the environment and its creatures. As such, with the use of natural processes, conservationists aim to control the ever-growing population.[[31]](#cite_note-33)[[28]](#cite_note-:3-30) In other places in [southern Africa](/wiki/Southern_Africa "Southern Africa"), the elephant population continues to increase.[[32]](#cite_note-34)
